chunks: The zakat al-fitr is obligatory — it is incumbent upon the man to pay it on behalf of himself and on behalf of every one of his dependants, from the young to the old, the free and the slave, the male and the female.

[He should pay] one sa'a of dates, or one sa'a of raisins, or one sa'a of wheat, or one sa'a of barley. The best of these is dates. One sa'a is four mudds, and one mudd is the weight of two hundred and ninety-two and a half dirhams. That equals one thousand one hundred and seventy dirhams in the Iraqi [weight].

There is no problem in paying its equivalent in gold or silver. There is no problem with one person paying on behalf of himself and those he supports all going to one recipient. It is not permissible to pay what is due from one person to two people.

There is no problem with paying the fitr from the first day of Ramadan until its end. It remains a zakat until one prays the Eid prayer; if one gives it after the prayer, it becomes a voluntary charity (sadaqa). The best time for it is the last day of Ramadan.

Whoever has a Muslim slave or a dhimmi [non-Muslim protected person] should pay the fitr on his behalf. Whoever has a child born on the day of Eid al-Fitr before zawal (midday) should pay the fitr on his behalf; but if the child is born after zawal, no fitr is required. The same applies if a man converts to Islam before or after zawal — the ruling follows accordingly.

key_terms.الزوال: Zawal: the moment of midday when the sun crosses its zenith; a legal criterion in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.الصاع: Sa'a: a unit of volume equal to four mudds, used to measure the required quantity of food
key_terms.المد: Mudd: a unit of measure, here defined as 292.5 dirhams by weight in the Iraqi system
key_terms.زكاة الفطرة: Zakat al-fitr: obligatory alms-tax paid at the end of Ramadan before the Eid prayer
key_terms.صدقة: Sadaqa: voluntary charity, distinct from obligatory zakat

ai.seo_question: What are the rules of zakat al-fitr in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Amali of Shaykh al-Saduq (d. 381 AH) provides comprehensive Shia jurisprudential guidance on zakat al-fitr, the obligatory alms-tax at the end of Ramadan. It details who must pay, the acceptable commodities and their quantities, the timeframe for payment, the distinction between pre-prayer payment (zakat) and post-prayer payment (sadaqa), and rulings for newborns and new converts based on the zawal (midday). These rulings were transmitted in 368 AH during a Friday assembly, reflecting the mature Imami fiqh tradition compiled by al-Saduq.
